titre: “Five a Day”: The Slogan of a 1988 California Campaign
accroche: “Five a day” comes from a 1988 campaign. Observational studies associate a lower risk up to 800 g per day (600 g for cancer).
contenu_vulgarise:
Five fruits and vegetables a day: the formula has settled into kitchens, packaging, and schools. It seems to come from a curve that would stop at five. Its documented origin is different.

## A Campaign, Not a Measurement

In 1988, California's health department launches a multi-year social marketing campaign, “5 a Day – for Better Health!” Its authors describe its features: a simple, positive message centered on a behavior, eating five servings of fruits and vegetables a day as part of a diet low in fat and high in fiber; the mass media; a partnership between the health department and the fruit and vegetable industries and large-scale retail; messages at points of purchase.

In 1991, the American National Cancer Institute and the Produce for Better Health Foundation adopt the campaign nationwide. In 1994, more than 700 industry organizations and 48 states, territories, and the District of Columbia hold a license to it. In its authors' summary, the number five is part of the content of the campaign's message; the summary does not present it as the result of a measurement.

## What the Curve Says

A 2017 meta-analysis, led by Dagfinn Aune and his colleagues, brings together 95 prospective studies. It counts in grams per day. For 200 g more of fruits and vegetables, the relative risk is 0.90 for all-cause mortality, that is, about 10% lower risk, 0.84 for strokes, and 0.92 for cardiovascular disease. The risk reductions continue up to 800 g per day for the outcomes measured, except for cancer, where they stop at 600 g.

As a first approximation, since these are observational studies: the authors estimate that in 2013, 7.8 million premature deaths worldwide could be attributed to an intake below 800 g per day, if the associations are causal.

## A Floor, Not a Ceiling

Two benchmarks therefore circulate. The first is a campaign slogan. The second is the recommendation of a 2003 FAO/WHO report: reach at least 400 grams per day. The words are “at least.” Neither the slogan nor the press release presents this figure as the limit beyond which the benefit ceases.

Is a message made to describe the curve, or to be remembered?

repere.texte: The risk reductions observed continue up to 800 g of fruits and vegetables per day for all the outcomes studied except cancer (600 g).
repere.source: Aune et al., International Journal of Epidemiology, vol. 46, no. 3, 2017 (retranslated from the French; original wording not retrieved)

carte.punch: “Five a day” is the slogan of a 1988 campaign, not the limit of the benefit.
carte.idee: “5 a Day” was born in 1988 as a California social marketing campaign, in partnership with the fruit and vegetable industry. A 2017 meta-analysis associates a lower risk up to 800 g per day (600 g for cancer); FAO and WHO recommend at least 400 g.

quiz.question: Why can't “five a day” be read as the point where fruits and vegetables stop providing a benefit?
choix: Because the California campaign was a clinical study measuring the effect of five servings
Because it is a campaign slogan, and studies show risk still falling beyond it
Because the FAO/WHO experts set the useful maximum at 400 grams
Because the benefit concerns only cancer
quiz.explication: The number five appears in the message of a 1988 campaign, and the 2017 meta-analysis associates a lower risk up to 800 g per day. The California campaign was a social marketing program, not a clinical study; the experts set a minimum of 400 g, not a maximum; and cancer is the outcome where the decline stops earliest, at 600 g, without being the only one concerned.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who launches the “5 a Day” campaign in 1988, and with what partner?
choix: California's health department, in partnership with the fruit and vegetable industries and large-scale retail
The National Cancer Institute, alone, with no partner among the food industries or large-scale retail
The World Health Organization, in partnership with the United Nations and European governments
A California consumer association, entirely independent of the food industry
quiz_supplementaire.explication: California's health department launches the campaign in 1988 in partnership with the fruit and vegetable industries and large-scale retail; the National Cancer Institute adopts it nationwide only in 1991.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the 2017 meta-analysis led by Dagfinn Aune and his colleagues, what is the estimated relative risk of all-cause mortality for 200 additional grams of fruits and vegetables per day?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2017 meta-analysis, covering 95 prospective studies, associates 200 g more of fruits and vegetables per day with a relative risk of 0.90 for all-cause mortality, that is, about 10% lower risk.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 2003 FAO/WHO report recommend on fruit and vegetable intake?
choix: A maximum of 400 grams per day, beyond which risk would rise
An intake of at least 400 grams per day
An intake of exactly 800 grams per day, to match the 2017 meta-analysis
No precise figure, only a varied diet
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The WHO and FAO press release of March 3, 2003, recommends reaching at least 400 grams of fruits and vegetables per day: a floor, not a ceiling beyond which the benefit would cease.
